transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brought you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Yeah, um, well, I came in today because... for a while now, I’ve been pretty convinced that certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with. Which is a lot of clients, actually, because Cincinnati has a surprisingly robust arts scene. A lot of people don't realize that, you know? They think it's just chili and baseball, but the symphony is world-class. I took a client to the symphony just last month, a retired engineer, great guy, loves Mahler. We had this amazing dinner beforehand... 

But anyway, what I mean is, these people are sending me these little signals about my clients. Like through the invitations I get in the mail, or the specific panel topics at networking events, or even who happens to sit right next to me at these galas. Like at that Mahler concert, the seating was just too pointed. Speaking of seating, I really need to get a new office chair. The lumbar support on mine is completely shot, and when you're looking at portfolios for nine hours a day, your lower back just screams at you. I saw this ergonomic one online that looked pretty good, but shipping was ridiculous... 

Sorry, what was I saying? Right, the signals at the events. I try to be rational about it. Even when I tell myself it could just be a coincidence, you know, just random event planning or a fluke, I just can’t really let it go. It's just too specific to ignore.
How long have you been having these thoughts about people signaling information about your clients — has it been weeks, months, or longer?

I'd say it's been about two months. Yeah, two months, because I remember it started right around the time tax season finally wrapped up. Which, by the way, was an absolute nightmare this year. The new tax codes are just a massive headache to navigate, especially for my clients with diversified real estate holdings. I had to spend three whole weekends just reading up on the amendments. I usually like to spend my weekends at the farmer's market down at Findlay Market. Have you been? They have this artisan cheese stand that makes a smoked gouda that is just unbelievable. I tried pairing it with a fig jam I found at a boutique grocery store in Mt. Adams, and it completely elevated the flavor profile. Honestly, I could probably live on cheese and crackers if I didn't care about my cholesterol... 

Wait, sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the timeline. Yeah, the signals and the tracking, I've been noticing all of that for about two months now.
Over these past two months, have you noticed any changes in your mood or energy — like feeling unusually elated, needing much less sleep than usual, or having racing thoughts?

No, not really. I mean, my mood has been pretty normal, I guess. I haven't been feeling super elated or anything like that. And my sleep is... well, it's about the same as always. I usually try to get my full eight hours because if I don't, I just can't focus on the spreadsheets. Which reminds me, I actually need to update my Excel software. The version I'm running is from like three years ago, and it keeps crashing when I try to run these complex macros for my clients' retirement projections. It's so frustrating when you're right in the middle of a calculation and the whole screen just freezes. I called IT about it, but you know how they are. They put you on hold for twenty minutes listening to that awful elevator music. I don't know who picks the hold music for these companies, but it's always some terrible smooth jazz. I actually used to play the saxophone in high school. I wasn't great, but I could play a decent rendition of "Careless Whisper." My parents made me practice in the garage because it was so loud... 

Anyway, what was the question? Oh, right, my energy and stuff. No, I haven't noticed any weird energy spikes or racing thoughts or anything like that. Just the normal amount of stress from work, you know?
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to notice or hear?

No, I don't think so. I haven't heard any voices or seen things that aren't there. I mean, my hearing is pretty sharp, though. I can always hear when the barista at my local coffee shop messes up the espresso machine pressure. It makes this distinct, high-pitched hissing sound that just completely ruins the extraction. You know, coffee is actually fascinating when you get into the science of it. The TDS—total dissolved solids—has to be perfectly balanced, or else the flavor profile gets totally muddy. I bought this refractometer online a few months ago just to test the coffee I make at home. It’s wild how much the water quality in Cincinnati affects the brew. I ended up installing a reverse osmosis system under my kitchen sink, which was a whole ordeal because the plumbing in my apartment building is incredibly old. The super had to come up three times because I accidentally caused a minor leak in the unit below mine. The guy downstairs was actually pretty cool about it, though. He’s a landscape architect, and he was telling me about this new drought-resistant grass he’s been planting...

Wait, sorry. What were you asking me? Oh, right, voices and stuff. No, nothing like that. Just the normal sounds around me.
Over these past two months, have you noticed any change in how well you're able to do your job or keep up with your usual daily responsibilities compared to before?

I'm still working, yeah. But I guess my practice has gotten a bit smaller lately. I've been missing some follow-ups with clients, and I've been avoiding some of the public financial panels I usually speak at. It's just been harder to keep up the same level of client contact I used to manage. Honestly, I think part of it is just the sheer volume of emails I get every day. It's overwhelming. I tried setting up these automated rules in Outlook to sort them by priority, but the algorithm they use is so clunky. It keeps sending important emails from my biggest client straight to the junk folder. Which reminds me, I really need to unsubscribe from all those promotional emails. I bought one pair of running shoes online, and now I get three emails a day from them. I don't even run that much anymore. I used to do 5Ks pretty regularly, but I sort of fell off the wagon after I tweaked my knee playing tennis last summer. Tennis is so hard on the joints, especially if you're playing on hard courts instead of clay. I read an article once about how the impact on your knees is like three times your body weight with every step...

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, my job. Yeah, I'm still working, just having a little trouble keeping up with everything the way I used to.
Before these last two months, had you ever had similar suspicious feelings or unusual beliefs like this, even in a milder form, earlier in your life?

No, not really. I mean, before a couple of months ago, everything was pretty normal. I didn't have any weird feelings or think people were doing things to me. I was just focused on work and trying to get my new apartment set up. Moving is such a nightmare, honestly. I decided to rent a U-Haul and do it myself to save money, but I totally underestimated how heavy my solid oak dining table was. I got it at this estate sale in Oakley—it's a beautiful piece, mid-century modern, probably from the late 60s. The guy who sold it to me said it belonged to his grandfather who was a woodworker. Woodworking seems like such a relaxing hobby, just sanding things down and smelling the sawdust. I bought a whittling kit once during the pandemic, thinking I'd make little wooden animals, but I ended up just cutting my thumb and bleeding all over the instructions. The bandages I bought were those cheap ones that don't even stick if you get them slightly wet, which is so annoying when you have to wash your hands all the time... 

Anyway, sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, before these last two months. No, I haven't ever had anything like this happen before. This is all pretty new.

Has this whole experience—feeling suspicious of these signals and having trouble keeping up with work—been going on continuously for these two months, or did you notice any early signs or a gradual build-up even before that, like subtle changes in how you were thinking or functioning?

Well, actually, it wasn't just the last two months. Now that I think about it, these changes have really been building up since that arts nonprofit recognition I got, which was a little over two years ago. They gave me this heavy glass plaque for helping them restructure their endowment. It’s sitting on my desk right now. 

Glass is such a weird material, you know? It’s an amorphous solid, so it’s not really a true solid. I went down this massive rabbit hole on Wikipedia about glassblowing recently. Did you know they have to cool it down super slowly in a special oven called an annealer? If they just leave it out at room temperature, the thermal stress makes it shatter into a million pieces. My aunt had this beautiful Murano glass vase from Italy that just cracked right down the middle one winter because she left it too close to a drafty window. She was devastated. She tried to glue it back together with epoxy, but you could totally see the seam. Epoxy is so tricky to work with, it always gets everywhere and you can never wash it off your hands... 

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again. What did you ask me about? Oh, right, the timeline. Yeah, it wasn't sudden. The build-up started a little over two years ago, right around that nonprofit thing.

Over these past two years, aside from how you've been responding to these signals you've noticed, has your day-to-day functioning—like your relationships, self-care, and general motivation—stayed pretty much the same, or has it gradually declined in other ways too?

Well, it's definitely changed. I still get my work done in pieces, you know, but I just don't have the same spark I used to. Like, I'll leave client follow-ups sitting there, and I've been skipping out on jazz nights or my pickup basketball games, and I don't really even feel bad about it. It just is what it is. And when my friends ask what's going on, I just give them really short answers because talking just feels like way more effort than it should be. 

Speaking of basketball, they just repaved the court at the park near my place. They used this new kind of composite material instead of regular asphalt. It's supposed to be better for shock absorption, which is great because my knees aren't what they used to be. I watched this documentary on how they make those synthetic courts, and it's wild—they use recycled tires. It's actually a really cool way to reduce waste, considering how many tires just end up in landfills every year. Did you know it takes like 50 to 80 years for a tire to decompose? And sometimes they catch fire in these massive landfill fires that can burn for months because the rubber just smolders... 

Wait, what was I talking about? Oh, right, my day-to-day. Yeah, I just don't have the motivation for much anymore, and talking to people just feels exhausting.
Over these past two years, have you been feeling persistently sad, down, or hopeless, or experiencing feelings of guilt or worthlessness?

No, not really. I mean, I'm not sad or crying all the time or anything like that. I just feel kind of... flat, I guess. I don't feel guilty about anything, I just don't have the energy for it. 

Energy is a funny concept, though, right? Like, we think about it as this thing we have or don't have, but in physics, energy is never created or destroyed, it just changes forms. The First Law of Thermodynamics. I remember learning that in high school physics. Mr. Henderson was my teacher, he always wore these really loud, mismatched bow ties. He said he bought them all at thrift stores because he refused to pay more than two dollars for a piece of fabric that just sits on your neck. Thrift stores are getting so expensive now, though. You go in looking for a cheap sweater and it's like twenty bucks. It's because of all those people who buy vintage clothes and flip them online for a profit. I mean, I get the hustle, but it kind of ruins the whole point of a thrift store, you know? It's supposed to be affordable for people who actually need it, not just a sourcing ground for some influencer's Depop shop...

Anyway, sorry. What were you asking? Oh, right, feeling sad or guilty. No, I haven't really been feeling sad or hopeless, just kind of empty, like I said.

I decided to rent a U-Haul and do it myself to save money, but I totally underestimated how heavy my solid oak dining table was. I got it at this estate sale in Oakley—it's a beautiful piece, mid-century modern, probably from the late 60s. The guy who sold it to me said it belonged to his grandfather who was a woodworker. Woodworking seems like such a relaxing hobby, just sanding things down and smelling the sawdust. I bought a whittling kit once during the pandemic, thinking I'd make little wooden animals, but I ended up just cutting my thumb and bleeding all over the instructions. The bandages I bought were those cheap ones that don't even stick if you get them slightly wet, which is so annoying when you have to wash your hands all the time... 

Anyway, sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, before these last two months. No, I haven't ever had anything like this happen before. This is all pretty new.

inference.note: No prior psychotic history, no hallucinations, no mood symptoms, and the belief system remains a single encapsulated persecutory theme with only mild functional decline — this favors delusional disorder (F22) over schizophrenia, though schizophrenia (F20.9) remains possible given ICD-10's 1-month duration threshold and some social/occupational decline. Schizotypal disorder (F21) is ruled out as there is a clear delusional belief system rather than eccentric traits/odd thinking without frank delusions.

patient.answer:
Well, actually, it wasn't just the last two months. Now that I think about it, these changes have really been building up since that arts nonprofit recognition I got, which was a little over two years ago. They gave me this heavy glass plaque for helping them restructure their endowment. It’s sitting on my desk right now. 

Glass is such a weird material, you know? It’s an amorphous solid, so it’s not really a true solid. I went down this massive rabbit hole on Wikipedia about glassblowing recently. Did you know they have to cool it down super slowly in a special oven called an annealer? If they just leave it out at room temperature, the thermal stress makes it shatter into a million pieces. My aunt had this beautiful Murano glass vase from Italy that just cracked right down the middle one winter because she left it too close to a drafty window. She was devastated. She tried to glue it back together with epoxy, but you could totally see the seam. Epoxy is so tricky to work with, it always gets everywhere and you can never wash it off your hands... 

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again. What did you ask me about? Oh, right, the timeline. Yeah, it wasn't sudden. The build-up started a little over two years ago, right around that nonprofit thing.

inference.note: The extended timeline (over two years, not just two months) with associated functional decline supports both persistent delusional disorder and schizophrenia as ongoing possibilities; the tangential, circumstantial speech pattern raises consideration of mild disorganization consistent with schizophrenia, but absence of hallucinations and preserved reasoning on unrelated topics keeps delusional disorder plausible as well.

patient.answer:
Well, it's definitely changed. I still get my work done in pieces, you know, but I just don't have the same spark I used to. Like, I'll leave client follow-ups sitting there, and I've been skipping out on jazz nights or my pickup basketball games, and I don't really even feel bad about it. It just is what it is. And when my friends ask what's going on, I just give them really short answers because talking just feels like way more effort than it should be. 

Speaking of basketball, they just repaved the court at the park near my place. They used this new kind of composite material instead of regular asphalt. It's supposed to be better for shock absorption, which is great because my knees aren't what they used to be. I watched this documentary on how they make those synthetic courts, and it's wild—they use recycled tires. It's actually a really cool way to reduce waste, considering how many tires just end up in landfills every year. Did you know it takes like 50 to 80 years for a tire to decompose? And sometimes they catch fire in these massive landfill fires that can burn for months because the rubber just smolders... 

Wait, what was I talking about? Oh, right, my day-to-day. Yeah, I just don't have the motivation for much anymore, and talking to people just feels exhausting.

inference.note: The 2+ year gradual decline with negative symptoms (avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal, blunted affect) and persistent circumstantial/tangential thought process alongside fixed delusions favor schizophrenia over delusional disorder, which typically preserves functioning and lacks these additional negative/disorganized features. F22 is ruled out given the significant functional deterioration and negative symptoms.

doctor.intent: To assess whether the avolition, anhedonia, and social withdrawal are accompanied by depressive symptoms (sadness, hopelessness, guilt), which would suggest a mood disorder with psychotic features rather than primary negative symptoms of schizophrenia.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I mean, I'm not sad or crying all the time or anything like that. I just feel kind of... flat, I guess. I don't feel guilty about anything, I just don't have the energy for it. 

Energy is a funny concept, though, right? Like, we think about it as this thing we have or don't have, but in physics, energy is never created or destroyed, it just changes forms. The First Law of Thermodynamics. I remember learning that in high school physics. Mr. Henderson was my teacher, he always wore these really loud, mismatched bow ties. He said he bought them all at thrift stores because he refused to pay more than two dollars for a piece of fabric that just sits on your neck. Thrift stores are getting so expensive now, though. You go in looking for a cheap sweater and it's like twenty bucks. It's because of all those people who buy vintage clothes and flip them online for a profit. I mean, I get the hustle, but it kind of ruins the whole point of a thrift store, you know? It's supposed to be affordable for people who actually need it, not just a sourcing ground for some influencer's Depop shop...

Anyway, sorry. What were you asking? Oh, right, feeling sad or guilty. No, I haven't really been feeling sad or hopeless, just kind of empty, like I said.

inference.note: Chronic (>2 year) course with persistent persecutory/referential delusions, prominent negative symptoms (avolition, affective flattening, anhedonia, social withdrawal), and functional decline, without mood episode symptoms, hallucinations, or manic/depressive features. Speech throughout the interview is markedly tangential/circumstantial with frequent loose associations, indicating formal thought disorder. Mood episodes (mania, depression) and hallucinations were explicitly denied, and no substance/medical cause was identified. The combination of delusions plus disorganized speech plus negative symptoms with functional decline over >6 months meets criteria for schizophrenia rather than delusional disorder (which would not include disorganized speech/negative symptoms) or a mood/schizoaffective disorder (no manic/depressive episode present).
